units.d: Life first: be won by the love of Christ before you carry his love to the nations.
The Bible is my standard and the Spirit is my guide: go by the Lord’s command, in the Spirit’s power.
Then ministry: witness in daily life, cross cultures with the gospel, and overcome through prayer and suffering.
Build God’s system: sending churches, mission teams and multiplying disciples, until every nation worships.

lessons.title: All the Nations Blessed Through You
lessons.sub: Our God is a missionary God; we are blessed so that every people may be blessed
lessons.hear:
When many people hear the word “mission,” they picture a distant jungle and a missionary with a backpack, and they assume it is a job for a few professionals. But in the Bible, mission does not begin with a mission agency. It begins in the heart of God. Some two thousand years before Jesus was born, God said to Abram, “I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.” (Genesis 12:2) Then he promised, “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” (Genesis 12:3) Our God is a missionary God. Mission is not one program among many in the church; it is God’s own purpose to redeem the nations.

This promise has a striking backdrop. One chapter earlier, at Babel, people said, “let’s make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4). They wanted to reach heaven on their own and build their own reputation. That is the self-centered old self: leaving our proper place, grasping for power, trying to take God’s place. In the very next chapter God turns it around: he himself will make Abram’s name great. A name is not seized; it is given. And God gives his blessing so that it will flow out to every people.

Israel has two lakes fed by the same Jordan River. The Sea of Galilee takes water in and lets it flow out, and it teems with fish. The Dead Sea only takes in; its salt builds up until almost nothing can live there. Many believers have been blessed, yet live like the Dead Sea: the gospel becomes their private insurance policy, and the church becomes their club. God never blesses us so we can hoard. He blesses us to make us channels.

Abram’s blessing began with leaving: “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.” (Genesis 12:1) For us, leaving may not mean moving overseas. It may mean stepping out of our comfort zone: greeting the coworker everyone ignores, welcoming the immigrant family that just moved in down the street, treating the caregiver from Indonesia or the Philippines in your home with real honor, answering an angry comment online with gentleness. Every person connected to you is one of the “families of the earth” God has placed in your life.

Paul later said that this promise was the gospel announced to Abraham in advance (see Galatians 3:8). It was fulfilled in Abraham’s descendant, Jesus Christ; the blessing the nations receive is Jesus himself. So the first step in a missionary’s life is not learning methods but being captured by this blessing. First we are won by the love of Christ; then we carry the love of Christ to the nations. Every grace you receive today has an address on it, and the address bears the name of someone who does not yet know Jesus.
lessons.light: The self-centered believer asks, “How will God bless me?” The selfless disciple asks, “Whom does God want to bless through me?” The builders of Babel made a name for themselves and were scattered; Abram let God be King, and every people was blessed through him. Blessing is not the finish line but the beginning of a channel. Let Jesus have all the glory, and the blessing will flow on.
think: Compare Genesis 11:4 with Genesis 12:2. How is “making a name for ourselves” different from God making our name great?
Am I more like the Sea of Galilee or the Dead Sea right now? Where has the grace I received flowed lately?
What comfort zone is God asking me to leave? Among my family, workplace and neighbors, who are the “families of the earth” God has placed near me?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you are a missionary God who planned from the beginning to bless all the families of the earth. I confess that I often think only about being blessed myself, and I store up your grace until it becomes a Dead Sea. Forgive me for trying to make a name for myself. Today I choose to let Jesus be King in my life and to become a channel of your blessing. Holy Spirit, open my eyes to the family members, coworkers and neighbors you have placed around me, so that the love I have received may flow to someone who does not yet know you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Count your blessings
Write down five blessings God has given you, and next to each one write the name of someone you could share it with.
Map your “families of the earth”
Draw three circles around yourself: family, workplace or campus, and neighbors and online friends. Write one to three names in each.
Start your Gospel Friends List
From your map, choose three to five people who do not yet know Jesus. Add them to your Gospel Friends List and pray for them every day.
Take one step out of your comfort zone
This week, show kindness to someone you would not normally approach, such as an immigrant neighbor, a foreign caregiver or a new coworker.
Pray for the nations
Spend three minutes each day praying for one country or people group, asking God that his “salvation among all nations” may be known (Psalm 67:2).
lessons.do: Today, write down three names: one family member, one coworker or classmate, and one neighbor or online friend. Add them to your Gospel Friends List and pray one minute for each. Then write one line in your Mission Journal: “The blessing God gave me today, I will let it flow to whom?”
deep: Isn’t mission only for a few missionaries? I’m not going overseas.

God’s promise to Abram was for “all the families of the earth,” and Jesus said, “As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.” (John 20:21) Every believer is sent. Some are called to long-term cross-cultural mission, but all of us are sent into our own homes, workplaces and neighborhoods. What sets a missionary apart is not location but whether life is flowing outward.
Does “blessed to be a blessing” mean Christians will always be prosperous and successful?

No. After his call, Abram went through famine, long waiting and severe tests of faith. The heart of biblical blessing is God’s presence and being used by God, not a success-gospel guarantee of wealth. The greatest blessing is Jesus Christ himself; when we bring him to people, we bring them the best blessing there is.
lessons.quick: Blessing is not the finish line but the start of a channel; God blesses you so the nations may be blessed through you.
text: Now the LORD said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
I will make of you a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing.
I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”
lessons.keyText: I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse him who treats you with contempt. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

lessons.title: Here I Am. Send Me!
lessons.sub: See the Lord’s glory and your own uncleanness first; then you will hear the call
lessons.hear:
Isaiah’s call comes with a date stamp: “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1). Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years and the nation had prospered, but late in life his heart grew proud. He barged into the temple to burn incense and was struck with leprosy (see 2 Chronicles 26:16-21). A king had left his proper place to seize authority that was not his, and a whole nation lost its sense of security. At that very moment Isaiah saw that the true King was still on the throne. Mission does not begin with seeing the need. It begins with seeing the Lord.

The seraphim called to one another, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3) God’s glory fills not only the temple but the whole earth; that itself is a missionary vision. Yet Isaiah’s first response was not “I’ll go.” It was, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). In a dim room you may think your clothes look fairly clean, but step into the noonday sun and every stain shows. The closer we come to the light, the more clearly we see ourselves.

This is where the selfless life begins. Someone who has never seen God’s glory can easily go out on mission with a sense of superiority: I know better than you; I have come to rescue you. But someone who has cried “Woe is me” before God knows that he is just like the people he serves, one who lives “among a people of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5), in equal need of mercy. Pride leaves its proper place and grasps for power; humility lays power down and returns to its place. Let people be people, and let God be God.

God did not leave Isaiah drowning in self-condemnation. A seraph took a live coal from the altar, touched his mouth and said, “your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.” (Isaiah 6:7) That altar fire points ahead to the cross. The coal cleansed an unclean mouth, and that very mouth was the one God would send to speak. God cleanses before he sends; he deals with our life before he entrusts us with ministry.

Then God asked, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8) This is not a draft notice but an invitation. Isaiah answered, “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8) He did not yet know where he was going or what he would do, but he gave himself first. The same question comes to you today. It may lead to a short-term trip to an unfamiliar country, or simply to a sincere word of care over lunch for a coworker who has just been through a painful breakup. “Here I am” speaks of position: I am right here before you. “Send me” speaks of lordship: you are King.
lessons.light: Self-centered mission starts with “I see the need and I have the ability,” and easily goes out to “rescue” people with an air of superiority. Selfless mission starts with “I have seen the Lord, and I need grace too,” and goes out to serve in humility. Our focus is on Jesus, not on our own zeal and not on other people’s needs. Only those who have said “Woe is me” before the Lord can sincerely say, “Send me.”
think: What did Isaiah see first, then what did he see about himself, and only then what did he hear? Why does this order matter?
Is there a hidden sense of “I’m better than you, I’ve come to save you” in the way I serve others?
When God asks today, “Who will go for us?” what condition or excuse rises first in my heart?
lessons.speak: Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies; the whole earth is full of your glory. Lord, before you I confess that I am a person of unclean lips. I often speak words of judgment, complaint and emptiness, and I often serve others with pride. Cleanse my mouth and my heart with the fire of the cross. I will not first ask where you are sending me; I give myself to you first. Lord, here I am. Send me! Be the King of my life, and let every word I speak carry your grace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Look to the throne first
Each day before you serve, spend five minutes meditating on Isaiah 6:1-3. Worship the Lord on the throne before you look at your to-do list.
Confess honestly
Write down one recent word of judgment, complaint or exaggeration. Confess it to God, and apologize to the person if needed.
Lay down superiority
Think of someone you long to see know Jesus, and write down three strengths in that person you could learn from.
Write My Salvation Story
In three parts, before I met the Lord, how I met the Lord, and since I met the Lord, write a testimony of about three minutes.
Offer yourself
In prayer, say, “Lord, here I am. Send me,” and hand him this week’s calendar to rearrange.
lessons.do: Today, find a quiet place and slowly read Isaiah 6:1-8 three times. The first time, worship God’s holiness. The second time, confess your own uncleanness. The third time, say to the Lord, “Here I am. Send me.” Then open My Salvation Story and write the first part: who I was before I met the Lord.
deep: I still have so many weaknesses and sins. Am I qualified to share the gospel?

Isaiah’s qualification was not “I am clean” but “God has cleansed me.” If we had to wait until we were perfect, no one could serve. Sharing the gospel is precisely testifying to how an unclean person has been cleansed by grace. What matters is coming to the cross daily to confess and repent and walking in the light. If there is a sin you keep committing knowingly, first open up to a spiritual elder and ask for help.
Does saying “Send me” mean I must quit my job and go overseas?

Not necessarily. “Send me” hands lordship to God; it does not set the location in advance. God may send you back to your family, keep you in your workplace as a light, or call you to cross-cultural service. If you sense a call to long-term mission, test it in prayer and confirm it together with your pastor, your spiritual parents and your sending church. Do not make a hasty decision on a passing feeling.
lessons.quick: See the Lord on the throne, then see your own uncleanness, and you will truly be able to say: Send me.
text: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew.
One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I live among a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!”
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar.
He touched my mouth with it, and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.”
I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”
lessons.keyText: I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am. Send me!”

lessons.title: The Love of Christ Compels Us
lessons.sub: No longer living for ourselves, we serve as Christ’s ambassadors
lessons.hear:
What could move a person to cross cultures, lay down a career and even face danger to share the gospel? Paul’s answer fits in one line: “For the love of Christ compels us” (2 Corinthians 5:14). The original word carries the sense of “holding tightly, pressing on.” Picture a river squeezed between two banks: the water rises, the current quickens, and it can rush in only one direction. The driving force of mission is not guilt, not pressure to produce results and not a need to prove ourselves. It is being gripped by the love of Christ.

The content of this love is the cross: “one died for all, therefore all died.” (2 Corinthians 5:14) Its purpose is “that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15) This is the shift from the self-centered old self to the selfless new self. The old life is like a drawing compass with its point stuck in “me”; every circle it draws goes around my achievements, my reputation, my comfort. The death of Christ pulls that point up and plants it in himself. From then on, life has a new center.

So Paul says, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17) A new creation even sees people differently: “we know no one according to the flesh from now on.” (2 Corinthians 5:16) We no longer size people up by education, income, nationality, accent or skin color. The foreign clerk on the night shift at the convenience store, the short-tempered boss, the stranger online who mocks your faith: Christ died for every one of them.

Then Paul gives us a new identity: “We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). An ambassador lives in a foreign land but represents the head of his own nation. His words are not personal opinions but official messages, and his conduct is his country’s calling card. At home, at the office and on social media, we are heaven’s embassy on location.

An ambassador’s work is to urge people to be reconciled to God, not to win debates or rack up numbers. Paul’s tone is a plea: “we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” (2 Corinthians 5:20) When we plead with gentleness, we will not pressure or manipulate, because people matter more than tasks and relationships matter more than things. Those compelled by love will never treat people as targets to hit; they see each one as someone the Lord loves. You do not need to rush to persuade anyone today. Just let your life become an open letter in which people can read that God, in Christ, is reaching out his hand to make peace with them.
lessons.light: The self-centered live for themselves, and even their ministry circles around their own achievements and reputation. The selfless are compelled by the love of Christ and no longer live for themselves but for the Lord. Self-centered witness is like sales, eager to close the deal; selfless witness is like an ambassador, pleading with people to be reconciled to God. Let Jesus be King. We are only messengers, and all the glory belongs to the King who sends us.
think: According to 2 Corinthians 5:14-15, what change does the death of Christ bring? What does “no longer living for myself” look like in my time, money and relationships?
“We know no one according to the flesh”: what kind of people am I most likely to judge by appearance, status or background?
How is an “ambassador” different from a “salesperson”? When I share my faith, which one am I more like?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for dying and rising again for me. Your love has taken hold of me. I confess that I still often live for myself, and even in serving I want people’s praise. Make me a new creation, so that I no longer regard anyone according to the flesh but see every person through your eyes. I want to be your ambassador and represent you at home, at work and online. Holy Spirit, give me gentleness and courage, so that without pressure or argument, with a pleading heart, I may urge people to be reconciled to God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Return to the source of love
Meditate on 2 Corinthians 5:14-15 each day, and write down one concrete way the love of Christ compelled you today.
Change the center
Look over this week’s calendar. Circle one plan that is about “living for myself” and replace it with something for the Lord and for others.
Put on new eyes
Choose someone you once looked down on because of appearance or background. Pray for that person, and take the initiative to interact with respect.
Be a worthy ambassador
Ask yourself: what kind of Jesus would people read in my words, my posts and my work attitude? Adjust one thing.
Practice gentle reconciling
Practice saying in two or three sentences to a gospel friend, “God wants to make peace with you.” Don’t argue; simply testify.
lessons.do: Today, write in your Mission Journal: “How did the love of Christ compel me today?” Then choose one person from your Gospel Friends List and show him or her the love of Christ in one concrete way: a phone call, a small snack or a sincere blessing. Don’t rush to explain doctrine; let the person experience being loved first.
deep: When I share the gospel and people reject it, or even react with hostility, did I do something wrong?

Not necessarily. An ambassador’s duty is to deliver the message faithfully; turning hearts is the Holy Spirit’s work. When Paul says “we beg you,” the very act of pleading acknowledges the other person’s freedom to respond. Examine whether your attitude was gentle and your timing wise, but do not carry the outcome on your own shoulders. Keep the relationship alive with love and entrust the person to God.
Should I wait until the relationship is very close before I urge someone to be reconciled to God?

Relationship is the bridge for the gospel, but once a bridge is built, someone has to walk across it. 321 says life first, then relationships, then ministry: our life is the witness, relationships are the channel, and at the right time we must explain the gospel clearly in words. You can begin by sharing your salvation testimony, then go step by step as the person opens up. If someone decides to follow Jesus, connect him or her to a church for nurture; the work does not end with the conversation.
lessons.quick: It is not guilt that pushes me but Christ’s love that holds me; I am an ambassador, not a salesperson.
text: For the love of Christ compels us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died.
He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.
Therefore we know no one according to the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no more.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
lessons.keyText: We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

lessons.title: Go and Make Disciples of All Nations
lessons.sub: Let Jesus be King: the heart of the Great Commission is disciples, not numbers
lessons.hear:
After the resurrection, the eleven disciples went up a mountain in Galilee. Matthew records a strikingly honest detail: when they saw Jesus they worshiped him, yet some still doubted (see Matthew 28:17). The Lord entrusted the mission that would change history not to flawless heroes but to ordinary people who were worshiping and wrestling at the same time. That is good news. You do not have to wait until your faith is perfect or your words are polished before you can be sent.

The first thing Jesus says is not a command but a declaration: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” (Matthew 28:18) Only then does he say, “Go and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19) Mission is not a grand plan we dream up for God; it is the order of a King. We go because Jesus already reigns. An ambassador carries credentials from his head of state, and his weight comes not from his own eloquence but from the one who sent him. To let Jesus be King is to admit that my family, my work, my time and my future all sit under his authority.

The Great Commission contains several actions: going, baptizing, teaching. But its backbone is one thing: making disciples. Going is the route, baptism is the starting line, teaching is the process, and disciples are the goal. A maternity ward counts births, but no parent thinks the job is done once the baby arrives; the real work is helping that child grow up. Many outreach efforts today focus on numbers: how many raised a hand, how many made a decision, how many clicked “like.” Numbers are not evil, but the moment people become performance figures, we have drifted from the Lord’s heart. Jesus said, “teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you.” (Matthew 28:20) The point is not merely knowing but obeying. A disciple is a life being changed by Jesus and learning to follow him day by day.

So the Great Commission does not belong only to missionaries. A brother who works at a tech company and reads a Gospel over lunch each week with two colleagues; a sister who has moved abroad and helps newly arrived immigrants with paperwork and language classes, slowly introducing them to Jesus. Both are making disciples of the nations. And today the nations live in our cities, our offices and our online communities.

Jesus ends with a promise: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:20) He is not standing at the finish line waiting to grade our results; he walks the whole road with us. The deepest secret of mission is not technique but presence. We invite people to follow the Lord who is walking with us right now.
lessons.light: The self-centered old self cares about numbers and reputation, treats people as results and casts itself as the hero. The selfless (no-self) life lets Jesus be King and sees each person as someone God loves, someone who needs companions to grow. We do not go to expand our own influence; we walk with people as they become disciples of Jesus, so that Jesus receives all the glory.
think: How does the declaration “All authority has been given to me” change your courage and your motives in sharing the gospel?
Do I care more about how many people make a decision, or about whether one person truly follows Jesus? What does the way I serve reveal?
Among my family, coworkers and neighbors, who are the one or two people God is asking me to walk with on the road of discipleship?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, all authority in heaven and on earth belongs to you. I confess that I often put my own plans at the center and measure ministry by numbers. Today I choose to let you be King of my life, to obey your command and to go where you send me. Place one or two friends on my heart. Make me willing not only to lead them to a decision, but to spend time reading Scripture and praying with them, learning together to obey your word. Thank you for promising to be with me always, so that I no longer need to be afraid or rely on myself. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Declare the Lord’s authority
Each morning before you leave home, read Matthew 28:18-20 and tell the Lord, “You are King. Send me.”
Write your Gospel Friends List
In your Gospel Friends List, write the names of three to five family members, coworkers or neighbors, and pray for them daily.
Start with a meal
Invite one friend from your list for a meal or a coffee. Care sincerely about their life, do not rush to preach, and build a genuine friendship first.
Read a Gospel together
Invite a willing friend to read a passage of Mark each week and discuss three questions: What does it say? What is Jesus like? How can I follow him?
Let the church help nurture
When a friend comes to faith, bring them into a small group or a new believers’ class. You are a companion, not their only shepherd.
lessons.do: Today, open your Gospel Friends List and write down one person you are willing to walk with on the road of discipleship for a year. Pray for them for three minutes. Then write in your Mission Journal: “Jesus is King. The small step I will take for this friend is…” and do it this week.
deep: Isn’t the Great Commission for pastors and missionaries? What does it have to do with an office worker like me?

Jesus spoke to all his disciples and promised to be with them to the end of the age, which shows that the command extends to believers in every generation. Missionaries are sent far away; every believer is sent into their own family, workplace and neighborhood. Your office may be the very field God has prepared for you.
Isn’t it enough to lead people to a decision? Why spend so much time making disciples?

A decision is a birth; discipleship is growing up. A baby who is born but never fed cannot survive, and faith that is never nurtured easily withers. You do not have to carry discipleship alone. Connect new friends to a small group, to spiritual parents and to the church family, so that the relationships of 235 walk with them together. Then their lives can take root and go on to multiply.
lessons.quick: The heart of the Great Commission is disciples, not numbers; not me as the hero, but Jesus as King.
text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.
lessons.keyText: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

lessons.title: You Will Receive Power When the Holy Spirit Comes
lessons.sub: The Holy Spirit is my guide: circle by circle, to the ends of the earth
lessons.hear:
Before Jesus ascended, the disciples gathered and asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6) They were thinking about national revival, political restoration and a timetable. Jesus gave them no date. Instead he turned their eyes from “when” to “by what power” and “to where”: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

First, look at the source of power. The newest smartphone, however powerful, is just a piece of glass without a charge. The disciples had walked with Jesus for three years, heard the best teaching and seen countless miracles, yet he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for what the Father had promised (see Acts 1:4). Mission does not run on enthusiasm, eloquence or strategy; it runs on the Holy Spirit. In 321 we say, “The Holy Spirit is my guide,” and “Rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head.” The Spirit gives us courage to speak, and he also leads us where to go and whom to speak to. On a desert road the Spirit told Philip to go and stay near a chariot (see Acts 8:26-29). One act of obedient nearness, and the gospel traveled toward Africa with an Ethiopian official.

Next, look at our identity: “witnesses.” A witness is not a lawyer who must win every argument. A witness simply tells honestly what he has seen and experienced. You do not need to be a theologian. You only need to be able to say, “This is who I was, and this is how Jesus has changed me since I met him.” That is the most powerful testimony there is.

Finally, look at the route. Throw a stone into a lake and the ripples spread out circle by circle. Jerusalem is the nearest circle: your family and the people you see every day. Judea is your city, your workplace, your school. Samaria is the group we feel distant from, even prejudiced against; for Jews of that day it was the last place they wanted to go. Today it might be new immigrants, migrant workers, or people whose views are the opposite of yours. The ends of the earth are all nations and peoples, including those who have never heard the gospel. These circles do not wait for the inner one to be finished. They unfold together: you can care for your family while praying, giving and joining short-term missions for distant peoples.

Samaria is often the hardest circle, because what we must cross is not distance but a wall in the heart. The Spirit’s power is not only power to work miracles; it is power to love people we never wanted to love. When we are filled with the Spirit, the prejudices of the old self are torn down, and the living water of the gospel flows out from us, circle by circle.
lessons.light: The self-centered old self wants to do great things for God with its own zeal and cleverness, yet stays inside its comfort zone. The selfless (no-self) life admits that apart from the Spirit it can do nothing, follows the Spirit’s leading, crosses the walls in the heart and loves those it never wanted to love. Our focus is not on our own ability but on the Spirit’s presence.
think: The disciples were preoccupied with “when,” but Jesus pointed them to the Spirit and to witness. What is my biggest concern about mission right now?
In my life, who is my Jerusalem, my Judea, my Samaria and my ends of the earth? Write down one person or group for each.
Which “Samaria” is the wall in my heart I least want to cross? How am I willing to ask the Holy Spirit to change me?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I need you. I confess that I often try to serve with my own zeal and cleverness, and I end up exhausted and more and more afraid. Come upon me and fill me, so that I receive power to be a witness for Jesus. Guide my steps, and show me whom to draw near to today and what to say. I also hand over to you the prejudices I hold against certain people. Tear down that wall, so that I can love those I never wanted to love. From my home to my city and to the ends of the earth, may the name of Jesus be lifted high. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Wait on the Spirit daily
Before you serve each day, be still for five minutes, ask the Spirit to fill you, and ask, “Lord, whom do you want me to draw near to today?”
Draw your circles
Draw four circles and write in each the people or groups that are your Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and ends of the earth.
Write My Salvation Story
In My Salvation Story, write three parts: before I met Jesus, how I met Jesus, and since I met Jesus. Keep it under three minutes.
Cross one wall
This month, get to know someone from a different background, such as a new immigrant, a foreign coworker or a migrant worker. Listen to their story first and respect their culture.
Pray for the ends of the earth
Use Pray for the Nations to pray for one people group or country each day. If God gives you a burden, ask your church how to join short-term missions or support sending.
lessons.do: Today, draw your four circles in your Mission Journal and write at least one name or group in each. Pray for one minute for each circle. Then be quiet and ask the Holy Spirit, “Whom should I draw near to first this week?” Write down the answer.
deep: I have not had any special spiritual experience. Can I still be a witness?

Yes. The Holy Spirit lives in every believer. The power of a testimony does not depend on how dramatic it is, but on how honest and real it is. A small story of how Jesus walked with you through a season of unemployment often touches hearts more than a big argument. Ask the Spirit to fill you every day and follow his gentle promptings, and you will find more opportunities than you imagined.
Do I need to lead my whole family to Christ before I care about people far away?

No. Jesus said “and,” not “then.” These circles unfold together. The early church bore witness in Jerusalem, and through persecution the gospel also reached Samaria (see Acts 8:4-5). Caring for your family is foundational, but you do not have to wait until everyone believes before you pray for the nations. At the same time, remember that going far away must never become a way to avoid your own family.
lessons.quick: The power for mission comes not from ourselves but from the Spirit, flowing out circle by circle to the ends of the earth.
text: Therefore, when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
lessons.keyText: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”

lessons.title: How Will They Preach Unless They Are Sent?
lessons.sub: Make the gospel clear: some go, some send
lessons.hear:
In Romans 10, Paul states the gospel with great clarity: “if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.” (Romans 10:9) The gospel is not vague positivity, nor a success formula that says believing in Jesus will make life go smoothly. It is good news with clear content. God created us and loves us. We have sinned and fallen short of God’s glory, and we are separated from him (see Romans 3:23). “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” and “he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4) We are called to repent, believe and receive Jesus as the Lord of our lives. Believing in the heart means placing the whole weight of our lives on him; confessing with the mouth means declaring publicly that from now on Jesus is Lord, not me.

Then Paul asks a chain of questions: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14-15) It is a chain written backwards: sent, preach, hear, believe, call. Picture an old bucket brigade passing water from a well to a burning house. If one person in the line stops, the well may be full but the fire never gets the water. God’s salvation is completely sufficient, yet he has chosen to let the gospel travel through human hands and human voices.

Many people around us have not rejected the gospel; they have simply never heard it clearly. Perhaps it is your parents, to whom no one has ever patiently explained it. Perhaps it is the young coworker who is active online but lonely inside. What they lack may not be information but someone willing to walk with them and say it plainly. So every believer should prepare a personal salvation story and learn to explain the heart of the gospel in simple words. Not a memorized script, but clear and sincere words that respect the other person’s response, without pressure or manipulation.

On this chain there are those who go and those who send. Not everyone must move far away, but everyone is on the line. Missionaries pass the buckets at the front; senders stand at the well, drawing water through prayer, giving and care. Remove any link, and the fire waits in vain.

Paul then quotes Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!” (Romans 10:15) Those feet are dusty, perhaps blistered, yet to people waiting for good news they are beautiful. Late at night, hungry and waiting for a delivery, you do not care whether the courier’s shoes are clean; you only care that he has finally arrived. Your words may not be eloquent, but when you carry Jesus to someone, heaven calls those feet beautiful.
lessons.light: The self-centered old self treats sharing the gospel as a matter of saving face, staying silent for fear of rejection or pushing people to decide in order to produce results. The selfless (no-self) life knows it is only a messenger; the focus is on Jesus, not on me. Our part is to say it clearly and live it out; it is the Holy Spirit who brings people to faith. We leave the results to God and give the glory to Jesus.
think: If I had only three minutes, could I explain the heart of the gospel clearly in my own words? Which part is hardest for me to explain?
On the chain of sent, preach, hear, believe and call, where am I standing right now?
Who around me may never have heard the gospel clearly? How can I become “beautiful feet” in that person’s life?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for sending your Son to die and rise again for me, so that I, a sinner, could believe in my heart, confess with my mouth and be saved. I confess that I often keep silent because I fear rejection or fear saying it badly, and I have forgotten to pray and give for missionaries. Forgive me. Holy Spirit, help me share the gospel clearly and gently, relying not on technique but on your love. Use my feet to go to those who have not yet heard, and use my hands to hold up the workers who have been sent. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: State the gospel in four points
Practice in your own words: God loves us; we have sinned and are separated from God; Christ died for us and rose again; we must repent, believe and receive Jesus as Lord.
Prepare My Salvation Story
Write a three-minute version in My Salvation Story, tell it to a spiritual companion first, and ask for feedback.
Practice the Six Steps
Role-play the Six Steps of a Gospel Conversation with a small group partner. Learn to listen before you share, and respect whether the other person wants to respond.
Become a sender
Adopt a missionary or a mission organization. Pray and give regularly, and send messages of care to them and their family.
Keep walking after a decision
If a friend wants to receive Jesus, pray with them, and within a week introduce them to a small group or a pastor to begin new believer care.
lessons.do: Today, write a three-minute version of My Salvation Story, read it aloud and time it. Then choose one person from your Gospel Friends List, ask the Lord to open a door, and look for a natural opportunity this week to show care and listen to their story.
deep: Isn’t it enough to be a good person and set a good example without saying anything?

Good deeds matter greatly; they make people willing to listen. But Paul asks how anyone can hear without someone to tell them. Our life is the loudspeaker and our words are the message; we need both. People can see love in us, but they need to hear from our lips that the source of that love is Jesus. Where law or culture places restrictions, share with even more wisdom, gentleness and respect, and pay attention to your own safety and the other person’s.
I can’t go to the mission field. Do I still have a part in mission?

Of course. Without senders there are no goers, and both matter equally. You can pray for one people group each day, give regularly to support missionaries, care for their families back home, and welcome international students and new immigrants near you. The nations have already come to us; the city you live in is itself a mission field.
lessons.quick: Your feet may be covered in dust, yet to those waiting for the gospel, they are beautiful.
text: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.
For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be disappointed.”
For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him.
For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?
And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!”
lessons.keyText: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?

lessons.title: Meeting Someone at a Well
lessons.sub: From a cup of water to living water that never runs dry
lessons.hear:
John tells us that on his way from Judea back to Galilee, Jesus had to pass through Samaria (see John 4:4). Many Jews would rather take a longer road than set foot there. But that “had to” was not on any map; it was in the Father’s heart. Someone was waiting at a well. Tired from the road, Jesus sat by the well at about noon (see John 4:6), the hottest hour, when a woman avoiding other people’s eyes came to draw water. Mission rarely begins at a pulpit; it begins at a well, on an ordinary afternoon, with a person who is trying not to be seen.

Jesus’ first words were not a sermon but a request: “Give me a drink.” (John 4:7) In one sentence he crossed three walls at once: ethnicity, gender and reputation. Astonished, she asked, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (John 4:9) Today the well might be the break room, the school gate, a park where migrant workers gather, or a thread online. We hurry to give people the gospel; Jesus first let her give him something, and she felt respected.

Then he moved from the water in front of them to water that lasts forever: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again” (John 4:13-14). The thirst of the human heart is like a phone battery: charge it to full today, and by tomorrow it is back in the red. Success, romance, shopping, binge-watching: we drink, and we thirst again. Jesus did not despise her thirst; he made her most ordinary need a door to living water. Good gospel conversation does not force the subject; it listens for the other person’s “water jar” and gently points to the Spring.

Jesus knew she had had five husbands, yet he did not condemn her. He spoke the truth inside grace, the way a doctor names an illness in order to heal, not to shame. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him (see John 3:17). We are tempted to win arguments; Jesus cared about winning a person. People matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. A gospel friend is not a sales target but someone God loves.

The story ends this way: “So the woman left her water pot, went away into the city” (John 4:28). A woman who hid from the crowd became a woman who invited the crowd: “Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done.” (John 4:29) She was no theologian. She simply told how she had been fully known and yet fully welcomed, and the whole town came out to meet him. You need not be eloquent; just stop at the wells of everyday life and say honestly, “He changed me.” Jesus is my example: as he met someone at a well, so we meet people in ordinary life.
lessons.light: The self-centered witness rushes to finish a prepared speech and treats people as targets to be conquered. The selfless witness sits down at the well like Jesus, lowers himself, listens first, and then points the place of thirst toward living water. Our focus is on Jesus, not on our eloquence and not on the other person’s response. It is the Holy Spirit who gives new birth; I am simply the one who offers a cup of water and points to the Spring.
think: In John 4:7-15, which walls did Jesus cross? How did he begin this conversation?
Where are the “wells” in my everyday life? Who around me is “drawing water at noon,” avoiding people yet longing to be seen?
What is the “water jar” of one gospel friend in my life? How could I move naturally from that need to living water?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for taking the road others refused to take, and for sitting at a well to wait for a woman everyone had forgotten. You once waited for me like that too. I confess that I am often quick to speak and slow to listen, quick to judge others in my heart and slow to remember the grace you have shown me. Open my eyes to see the wells in my daily life and the thirsty people beside them. Holy Spirit, give me a humble heart and gentle words, so that I can move from people’s needs to you, the Spring of living water. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Find your wells

Write down three places where you regularly meet people each week, such as the break room, the school gate or a neighborhood group chat, and ask the Lord to arrange encounters there. If the person is of the opposite sex, talk in a public setting or ask a same-sex co-worker to follow up.
Ask for a cup of water first
Ask a gospel friend for advice or a small favor, so that he or she feels respected and the relationship begins on equal ground.
Listen for their thirst
In conversation, ask more and talk less. Notice the pressures, regrets or longings the person keeps coming back to, and record them in your Gospel Friends List as a guide for prayer.
Move from water to living water
Prepare a natural bridge, such as, “I’ve struggled with that too, and I found strength in my faith,” then share your salvation testimony in three minutes.
Invite, don’t pressure
If your friend is interested, invite him or her to read John 4 with you or to visit your small group. If not, respect that decision, keep being a friend and keep praying.
lessons.do: Today, open your Gospel Friends List and write down one person you often meet at one of the “wells” of your daily life. Pray for that person for three minutes. Then reach out with a greeting or ask for his or her advice on something. Don’t rush to talk about faith; simply listen with genuine care. Tonight, record in your Mission Journal the “thirst” you heard.
deep: I’m not a good speaker and I don’t know the Bible well. Can I still share the gospel?

The Samaritan woman had believed for less than a day and had no training at all. She simply said, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I have done” (John 4:29), and the whole town came out to meet Jesus. The power of the gospel is not in eloquence but in Jesus himself. Your most powerful tool is your salvation testimony: who I was before, how I met the Lord, and how my life has changed since. Write it down, practice telling it in three minutes, and leave the rest to the Holy Spirit.
If someone’s life is clearly sinful and I don’t point it out, am I compromising?

Jesus did bring up the woman’s five husbands, so not condemning is not the same as never talking about sin. The difference lies in order and motive. He built the relationship first and let her feel accepted, then spoke the truth inside grace, aiming to heal rather than to shame. Our role is to point to Jesus and let the Holy Spirit convict the conscience (see John 16:8). We must not replace the gospel with moral judgment, nor change the gospel to please people.
lessons.quick: Stop at the wells of everyday life, and move from people’s thirst to the living water of Jesus.
text: A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”
For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.
The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. So where do you get that living water?
Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his children and his livestock?”
Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I don’t get thirsty, neither come all the way here to draw.”
lessons.keyText: but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”

lessons.title: All Things to All People
lessons.hear:
Paul was a Roman citizen, highly educated and an apostle, with plenty of rights to insist on. Yet he wrote, “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.” (1 Corinthians 9:19) A free man choosing to become a servant is the most beautiful paradox of mission. Picture a concert pianist teaching children in a village school. He does not insist on Chopin; he crouches down and starts with nursery songs. He has not lost his gift; he has simply lowered himself for the children.

The source of this kind of mission is Jesus himself. The Word became flesh and lived among us (see John 1:14); he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:7) God did not drop an instruction manual from heaven; he came in person, into human language, food and suffering. This is incarnational mission: not requiring others to become like us before they deserve to hear the gospel, but stepping into their world first. For an immigrant coworker, it may mean learning to pronounce his name correctly; for a teenager, shooting hoops with him; for an elderly neighbor, patiently hearing her stories to the end.

But this is not being a chameleon or having no convictions. Paul adds, “not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). People in mission must tell two things apart: the gospel and culture. The gospel is the core, and it cannot change: Christ died for our sins, was buried and rose on the third day (see 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Culture is the vessel, and it can change: the style of worship music, the time of meetings, whether we eat with chopsticks or with our hands. A common mistake is exporting our culture along with the gospel. The opposite is surrendering the truth in order to be accepted.

This requires not technique but a selfless life. The self-centered old self says, “My way is more spiritual.” That is pride: leaving our proper place and putting our own culture on the throne. The selfless person returns to his proper place, lets people be people and lets God be God, and acknowledges that every people group is made in the image of God. Paul says, “To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.” (1 Corinthians 9:22) His focus is not on being liked, but on saving some.

Finally, Paul reveals his motive: “Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.” (1 Corinthians 9:23) People in mission are not spectators throwing life rings from the shore; they jump into the water and are held up by the gospel together with others. When you adjust a team meal for a foreign coworker or translate church jargon for a seeking friend, you are living out Jesus’ example: laying yourself down in order to win people.
lessons.light: Self-centered mission wants others to become like me before I will hand them the gospel. Selfless mission follows the incarnate Jesus, setting aside my own habits and rights and stepping into someone else’s world. Culture can yield; the gospel cannot change. I can stoop low, but the truth must not shrink. Let people be people, let God be God, and let Jesus receive all the glory from every nation and people.
think: In 1 Corinthians 9:19-23, what rights did Paul set aside in order to win people? What did he refuse to let go of?
Have I, without realizing it, treated my own cultural habits (language, clothing, style of meeting) as part of the gospel?
Who around me is “very different from me” (in nationality, generation, social class or religious background)? What could I lay down for that person, and what could I learn?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, though you existed in the form of God, you willingly emptied yourself, took the form of a servant and lived among us. I confess that I often want others to live my way, and I value my own habits more than people. Tear down the pride and prejudice in me and give me a servant’s heart. Holy Spirit, teach me to discern what is the gospel and what is only culture, so that I may become all things to all people, for no other reason than to win them to you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Draw your culture map

Write down three people around you whose cultural background differs from yours, such as a new immigrant, a coworker from another country or a neighbor from a different generation. Each of them is one of your “2,” so write a one-sentence prayer for each.
Learn their language
Learn a greeting in the person’s mother tongue, pronounce his or her name correctly, or find out about one of their festivals, showing respect through action.
Separate gospel from culture
List three things in your own or your church’s habits that are “culture that can be adjusted,” and three that are “the gospel core that cannot change.”
Translate the jargon
Practice sharing the gospel without church words like “saved,” “born again” or “repent,” using language your friends actually understand.
Respect and stay within bounds

Before cross-cultural service, learn the local laws, customs and safety guidelines. Whenever minors or restricted regions are involved, always work together with your church and mission agency, and never act alone.
lessons.do: Today, choose one person whose cultural background differs from yours and take the initiative to learn one thing about him or her: the meaning of a name, a dish from home or a festival. Add that person to your Gospel Friends List, and in Pray for the Nations, pray once for the people group he or she belongs to.
deep: Doesn’t “all things to all people” risk drifting with the crowd and compromising to fit in?

Paul’s flexibility has a clear boundary: he is “under law toward Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21). Whatever Scripture clearly forbids, such as idolatry, lying or immorality, we must never do in order to fit in. Whatever is culturally neutral, such as food, clothing, language and the rhythm of life, we may adjust out of love. The question to ask is this: does this help people see Jesus more easily, or does it blur the truth of the gospel?
I haven’t gone overseas. What does cross-cultural mission have to do with me?

Today the nations have already come to us: migrant workers, new immigrants, international students, coworkers from other countries. The internet has us crossing cultures every day. Between generations and social classes there are invisible cultural walls as well. In your office, your neighborhood and your children’s school, you can practice incarnational mission. And if God one day calls you far away, today’s practice will be your best preparation.
lessons.quick: Culture can be laid down, but the gospel cannot change; the lower we stoop, the more people we can win.
text: For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.
To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law;
to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law.
To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.
Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.
lessons.keyText: To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.

lessons.title: The Harvest Is Plentiful, the Laborers Few
lessons.sub: See with Jesus’ eyes before you walk in Jesus’ steps
lessons.hear:
Matthew leaves us a snapshot of Jesus’ itinerary: “Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.” (Matthew 9:35) Yet what Matthew records next is not a report of results but the look in Jesus’ eyes: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.” (Matthew 9:36)

Picture a crowded subway platform at rush hour. One person sees congestion and the risk of being late. Jesus sees people who are harassed and scattered: the office worker heading home near midnight, the teenager scrolling until he cannot sleep, the migrant worker missing her children over a video call, the newcomer starting life over in a foreign land. The word for compassion describes a pain felt deep in the gut. On a spreadsheet a crowd is a number; in Jesus’ eyes it is a flock of lost sheep. Mission begins with the eyes. Change how you see, and your feet will follow.

Then Jesus said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” (Matthew 9:37) He did not say the enemies are many or the obstacles great. He said the harvest is plentiful; the fields are ripe. Imagine an orchard owner looking at trees heavy with ripe mangoes. His worry is not a shortage of fruit but a shortage of pickers. One more week, and the fruit will rot on the ground. The problem has never been the harvest. It is the workers.

Jesus’ remedy is surprising. He does not begin with a recruitment rally; he begins with prayer: “Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.” (Matthew 9:38) The harvest belongs to the Lord, and so does the sending. To pray this way is to let Jesus be King, confessing that the harvest is in his hands, not in our strategies or our zeal. The word for “send out” can mean “thrust out,” and this prayer often moves the one who prays it. In the very next chapter, the disciples who were told to pray are themselves sent out (see Matthew 10:1-5). Many missionaries tell the same story: they began by praying for one people group, God placed that people in their hearts, and in the end he sent them there.

So this is a dangerous prayer, and a blessed one. Start today with five names on your Gospel Friends List. Pray for them every day, pray for the nations, and then add one line: “Lord, if you are willing, send me too.” He may send you to the next desk at work, to a stall in the market, to the comments section online, or one day to the ends of the earth. “Laborer” is not a title for a few professionals. It belongs to every disciple who has been moved by the Lord’s compassion and is willing to say, “Here I am.”
lessons.light: The self-centered person looks at a crowd and sees a nuisance, competition or targets to hit. The selfless person looks through Jesus’ eyes and sees harassed, scattered sheep who need a shepherd. The self-centered rush to bring in the harvest by their own methods; the selfless first kneel before the Lord of the harvest. The harvest is his, the authority is his and the glory is his; I am simply a laborer he sends.
think: When Jesus saw the crowds, he “was moved with compassion for them.” In the crowds I pass every day, who is “harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd”?
Do I tend to blame the soil, such as hard hearts or hostile surroundings, for the difficulty of sharing the gospel, or do I admit that the real shortage is laborers?
If I sincerely ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers, am I willing for him to send me? What holds me back?
lessons.speak: Lord of the harvest, thank you for having compassion on me when I was harassed and scattered, and for becoming my Shepherd. Open my eyes to see the people around me as you see them: my family, my coworkers, my neighbors and those who are far from home. I confess that I often see only busyness and inconvenience, and miss the harvest that is already ripe. Lord, send out laborers into your harvest; and if you are willing, send me too. Let me serve not by my own zeal but by your compassion and the leading of your Spirit, as a faithful laborer in your field. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Put on new eyes

This week, stop for five minutes in a crowded place, such as a train station, a market or the office cafeteria. Ask the Lord to show you one person who is “harassed and scattered,” and note it in your Mission Journal.
Write five names
On your Gospel Friends List, write the names of five people who do not yet know Jesus, including family, coworkers and neighbors, and pray for them by name every day.
Pray for laborers on schedule
Set a daily phone reminder for 9:38 and pray Matthew 9:38: ask the Lord to send laborers to your home, your workplace, your city and the nations.
Adopt a people group
Choose one country or unreached people group in Pray for the Nations, and for one month pray for its church, its missionaries and open doors for the gospel.
Put yourself on the prayer list
Each time you pray for laborers, end with, “Lord, here I am; send me too,” and watch for the nudges and opportunities the Spirit gives.
lessons.do: Today, write five names on your Gospel Friends List and pray Matthew 9:38 over them: “Lord of the harvest, send laborers to their side.” Then be still for one minute and ask the Lord, “To whose side are you sending me first?” Write the answer in your Mission Journal.
deep: If salvation is God’s work, why do we still need to pray and share the gospel?

God’s sovereignty does not cancel our prayers; it is the very ground of them. Because the harvest belongs to the Lord, we ask the Lord of the harvest. Because God is the one “who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), we can pray with confidence. God has ordained the end and also the means to that end: people who pray and people who are sent. Prayer does not twist God’s arm; it aligns our hearts with his.
I’m not a pastor and I’m not a gifted speaker. Is being a “laborer” really for me?

Yes. Jesus spoke these words to all his disciples, not only to apostles or pastors. Laborers depend not on eloquence but on compassion and obedience. One person bears witness through honesty at the office; another welcomes neighbors around the dinner table; another prays and gives online for missionaries far away. God sends each of us differently, but every disciple belongs in the harvest crew.
lessons.quick: See the crowds with Jesus’ eyes, pray with Jesus’ heart, then let Jesus send you.
text: Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.
Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”
lessons.keyText: Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”

lessons.title: Singing Hymns at Midnight
lessons.sub: In the darkest night, praise is the loudest witness
lessons.hear:
Paul and Silas came to Philippi because of a vision: a man of Macedonia begging them to come over and help (see Acts 16:9-10). They obeyed. And what happened? After they cast a spirit out of a slave girl, they were falsely accused, stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into prison, their feet fastened in the stocks (see Acts 16:19-24). Obeying God does not guarantee smooth sailing. Many believers know this firsthand: they followed God’s leading, only to face job loss, misunderstanding, a rejected visa or opposition from their own family.

Then comes one of the most moving scenes in Acts: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” (Acts 16:25) Midnight is the darkest hour, when wounds hurt most. They did not complain and they did not curse; they sang. The stars are in the sky all day long, yet only the darkest night lets people see them. Joy in good times is nothing unusual; praise in suffering makes people listen. Your coworkers and family are listening too. When you lose your job, fall ill or are wrongly accused, what comes out of your mouth: complaint or praise?

Then God moved: “Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.” (Acts 16:26) Praise is not an anesthetic; it turns our focus from our circumstances to the God on the throne. More remarkable still, the doors were open and Paul did not leave. The jailer, thinking the prisoners had escaped, drew his sword to kill himself, and Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!” (Acts 16:28) Those words shook the jailer more than the earthquake: the men he had locked in the stocks cared about his life. Mission is not seizing the chance to escape; it is seeing the person within the chance. People matter more than projects.

So the jailer asked the most important question there is: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30) The answer was simple and clear: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:31) Then “they spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.” (Acts 16:32) That same hour of the night he washed their wounds, and he and all his household were baptized (see Acts 16:33). From enemy to brother, from prison cell to dinner table, he “rejoiced greatly with all his household, having believed in God.” (Acts 16:34)

Your midnight may be a diagnosis or a layoff notice. Don’t waste your midnight. This is exactly when God wants to use your praise, and the person quietly listening nearby may belong to the very household God intends to save.
lessons.light: The self-centered person in suffering sees only his own wounds and keeps asking, “Why me?” with his focus fixed on circumstances. The selfless person still praises at midnight, because his focus is on Jesus. The self-centered bolt the moment the door opens; the selfless stay behind, caring for the very man who guarded them. Praise lets Jesus be King, and even a prison becomes a pulpit for the gospel.
think: Paul and Silas ended up in prison because they obeyed God. When I obey God and then meet hardship, what is my usual first reaction?
In my present “midnight,” who around me is listening? What do they hear from me: complaint or praise?
The doors opened, yet Paul stayed to save the jailer. Have I ever missed a chance to see and rescue someone because I was looking after my own convenience?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the light in the night. I place my midnight in your hands: the wounds, the stocks that hold me, the things I cannot see a way through. I do not want to be absorbed in my own pain. Give me a new song, so that even in the dark I keep praising you. May my family, coworkers and neighbors who are listening hear your faithfulness through my life. Give me a heart that cares for people, one that does not rush out when the door opens but is willing to stay for someone’s salvation. Let your salvation come to their whole household. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Prepare a midnight song
Find a worship song that carries you through hard times. Save the lyrics on your phone and sing or pray them in your hardest moments.
Count grace in hardship
During a difficult season, write down three things to thank God for each day, turning your focus from circumstances back to Jesus.
Prepare a three-minute testimony
Use My Salvation Story to shape your story: life before Christ, how you came to faith and how he has changed you, so you are always ready to answer, “What must I do to be saved?”
Pray for a whole household
Choose one person from your Gospel Friends List and pray not only for him or her but for each family member by name.
Hand new believers to the church

If someone decides to follow Jesus, help him or her connect with a local church for baptism and discipleship, so new life is not left alone. When sharing with minors, respect and inform their parents.
lessons.do: Today, write down one difficulty you are facing, and beside it write three sentences of praise to God. Sing a song of worship to him. Then ask yourself: in this situation, who is listening? Pray for that person and his or her whole household, and record it in your Mission Journal.
deep: Does “you and your household” mean that if I believe, my whole family is automatically saved?

No. This is the gospel promise opened to the whole household, not one person believing on behalf of the others. The passage goes on to say that “they spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house” (Acts 16:32); the whole household heard the word and believed in God. Each person must believe for himself or herself. Yet this verse gives us great hope: God values families, and he often begins with one person to save an entire home. So keep praying for unbelieving family members and keep living out your witness, never giving up and never forcing.
Isn’t praising God in suffering just suppressing real pain and pretending to be strong?

Biblical praise never asks us to pretend. Paul and Silas still had bleeding backs, and they were both praying and singing: pouring out their wounds to God and declaring their faith in him. Many psalms begin in lament and end in praise. True praise does not deny pain; it declares in the middle of pain that God is greater than my situation. If the wound runs very deep, seek the companionship of spiritual friends and qualified professionals as well.
lessons.quick: Don’t waste your midnight: praise in suffering is the loudest gospel.
text: But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”
He called for lights, sprang in, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas,
brought them out, and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.
He took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household.
He brought them up into his house and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly with all his household, having believed in God.
lessons.keyText: They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

lessons.title: The Holy Spirit Said, “Separate Them for Me”
lessons.sub: Some go and some send, all within one sending
lessons.hear:
The church in Antioch had an unremarkable beginning. Believers scattered by persecution arrived there and “spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus.” (Acts 11:20) Barnabas was sent to them, and he went on to Tarsus to find Saul. “For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” (Acts 11:26) Seeds scattered by persecution grew into the first church to send missionaries into the Gentile world.

Look at the church’s leadership team: “Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.” (Acts 13:1) Barnabas came from Cyprus. “Niger” means “black,” so Simeon may well have come from Africa. Lucius was from Cyrene in North Africa. Manaen grew up in a royal court. Saul had once persecuted the church. Different in ethnicity, skin color, class and past, they served with one heart. In an orchestra every instrument sounds different, yet every player watches the same conductor. A mission team is itself a witness to the gospel: only the cross can bring people like this together.

How did the sending happen? “As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.’” (Acts 13:2) Not in a strategy meeting, but in worship and fasting. Mission begins not with a need but with God’s voice and the Spirit’s leading. Notice the words “for me.” Missionaries belong to God, not to themselves, and the work is the work “to which I have called them.” The authority is God’s.

What is remarkable is that the church sent out its two best leaders. In their place we might have asked, “If they leave, what will happen to our church?” A selfless church does not keep its best for itself; it gives its best to God. “Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.” (Acts 13:3) The laying on of hands means identification and blessing, and sharing the same yoke. Yet the next verse says they were “sent out by the Holy Spirit” (Acts 13:4). The church released them; the Spirit sent them. Human obedience and divine sovereignty meet in one act.

Mission is like climbing a great mountain. The climbers who reach the summit are the ones people see, but the base camp and the voice on the other end of the radio are just as much part of the expedition. Some go and some send; those who send hold the goers up with prayer, giving and care. Later Barnabas and Saul returned to Antioch and reported to the church all that God had done through them (see Acts 14:26-27). They had never left the team. You may not be the one who climbs, but you can be the base camp, letting everyone who is sent know that they are not fighting alone.
lessons.light: A self-centered church wants to keep its best people and build its own size; a selfless church gives its best to God and builds God’s Kingdom. A self-centered missionary thinks, “Those who go are the greatest,” and a self-centered church member thinks, “Mission has nothing to do with me.” The selfless know that those who go and those who send share one sending and one team, and all the glory belongs to the God who sends us.
think: The church in Antioch heard the Spirit’s voice while they “served the Lord and fasted.” How often do my small group and I quietly and intentionally wait for the Spirit’s direction?
Antioch’s leaders came from different peoples and backgrounds. How can my team live out a witness of being different yet one in heart?
Between those who go and those who send, where is God placing me right now? How can I concretely hold up one missionary?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit who sends, like the church in Antioch we want to listen quietly for your voice as we worship and fast. Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening. I do not want to cling to the people, time and money I have; whatever you would set apart, I willingly offer. If you want me to go, I will go; if you want me to send, I will faithfully hold up those who are sent with prayer, giving and care. Make our team one in heart though we are different, so that the world may recognize you in our unity. May all the glory be yours. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
prac: Set aside time to fast and pray
Agree with your small group or a spiritual companion to fast for a meal or a day. Worship together and ask the Lord, “Whom are you setting apart? What are you sending us to do?”
Adopt a missionary
Get to know one missionary your church sends or supports. Write down the missionary’s name, field and prayer requests, and pray for him or her and the family every week.
Give regularly to missions
Set aside a regular gift for missions. It need not be large, but let it be a sign of your share in the sending.
Write a letter of care
